title: Thanks that names the thing
description: “Thanks for everything” warms no one; thanks that names the exact thing lands like it was aimed.

body.heading: Specific beats grand
paragraphs: Compare “Thanks for your help” with “Thanks for staying late on Thursday to finish the rota — it meant I got to my daughter’s concert.” The second tells the person precisely which of their actions mattered, and therefore which ones to repeat. Vague thanks is weather; specific thanks is a map.
It also proves attention. Anyone can say thanks; only someone who noticed can say that.

body.heading: Name the cost, not just the gift
paragraphs: The deepest thanks acknowledges what the help cost: time, trouble, a rearranged plan. “I know you gave up your Saturday morning” tells the giver their sacrifice was seen, not just its result enjoyed. Being seen in the cost is often the part people remember for years.
This is also why specific thanks cannot be mass-produced. It requires having actually watched another person’s life for a moment.

body.heading: Say it while it is still warm
paragraphs: Thanks decays. The same words delivered a month later arrive as administration; delivered the same day, they arrive as joy. Build the reflex: notice, name, say — ideally before you have done anything else with the feeling.
And if you have missed the moment, send it late anyway with the date attached: “I still think about what you did in March.” Late specific thanks beats punctual vague thanks every time.

takeaway: Name the action, name its cost, and say it the same day if you possibly can.
